questions.question: Nadia draws a rectangle on centimetre grid paper. It covers 3 rows of squares with 4 squares in each row, with no gaps and no overlaps. What is the area of her rectangle?
questions.explain: Area is the number of square units that cover the shape: 3 rows of 4 squares = 12 squares, so 12 cm². The usual trap is counting the units around the outside (that gives 14, which is the perimeter) or writing cm instead of cm² — area is always measured in square units.

questions.question: A rectangular library poster is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its area?
questions.explain: For a rectangle, area = length × width, because the length tells you how many squares are in each row and the width tells you how many rows: 8 × 5 = 40 cm². Watch out — adding the sides (8 + 5 = 13) or going all the way around (26 cm) gives perimeter ideas, not area.

questions.question: A rectangular sticker has an area of 24 cm². One side is 6 cm long. How long is the other side?
questions.explain: Since length × width = area, you undo the multiplication with division: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cm, and you can check with 6 × 4 = 24 cm². The common trap is subtracting (24 − 6 = 18) or multiplying again (24 × 6), but the missing side must make the two sides multiply back to the area.

questions.question: Mr. Chan is building a fence right around his rectangular vegetable garden. The garden is 9 m long and 6 m wide. Fencing costs $4 for each metre. How much will the fencing cost?
questions.explain: A fence goes around the edge, so you need perimeter first: 9 + 6 + 9 + 6 = 30 m, then 30 × $4 = $120. The biggest trap is using area (9 × 6 = 54) for a fence question, and the second is forgetting that there are two long sides and two short sides.

questions.question: Four rectangular dog runs all use exactly 16 m of fencing, so they all have a perimeter of 16 m. Which run gives the dog the most space (the greatest area)?
questions.explain: Check each one: 3 × 5 = 15 m², 4 × 4 = 16 m², 2 × 6 = 12 m², 1 × 7 = 7 m², so the square 4 m by 4 m holds the most even though every run uses the same fencing. The trap is thinking the longest, stretchiest rectangle must have the most area — same perimeter does not mean same area, and the closer to a square, the bigger the area.

questions.question: On centimetre grid paper, Priya traces the leaf she found at the park. Her tracing covers 9 full squares, and 4 more squares are each covered exactly half way. What is the best estimate of the area of the leaf?
questions.explain: Count the full squares, then join the half squares in pairs: 4 halves make 2 whole squares, so 9 + 2 = 11 cm². The two traps are counting every part-covered square as a whole one (13 cm²) or throwing the halves away (9 cm²) — half squares still cover real space.

questions.question: The Grade 5 class is planting a rectangular garden bed beside the school. The bed has an area of 48 m² and its length is 8 m. The class wants to put wooden edging all the way around the bed. How many metres of edging do they need?
questions.explain: First find the missing width from the area: 48 ÷ 8 = 6 m; then go around the whole bed: 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 m. Students often stop after one step and answer 14 m (just one long side plus one short side) or reuse the area number 48 — edging follows the perimeter, so every one of the four sides has to be counted.

questions.question: Jayden says, ‘If two gardens have the same area, they must need the same amount of fencing.’ Which example shows that Jayden is wrong?
options: A 6 m by 6 m garden and a 4 m by 9 m garden both have an area of 36 m², so both need 24 m of fencing.
A 5 m by 5 m garden has more area than a 2 m by 8 m garden, so it must need more fencing.
A 6 m by 6 m garden and a 4 m by 9 m garden both have an area of 36 m², but one needs 24 m of fencing and the other needs 26 m.
A 3 m by 6 m garden has an area of 18 m² and a perimeter of 18 m, so area and perimeter are really the same thing.
questions.explain: To disprove a claim you need one true example that breaks it: 6 × 6 = 36 m² with perimeter 24 m, and 4 × 9 = 36 m² with perimeter 26 m — same area, different fencing. The trap is believing area and perimeter always grow together; they measure different things (space covered versus distance around), so a 5 m by 5 m and a 2 m by 8 m garden can even have the same perimeter of 20 m with very different areas.
